newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: U.N. human rights mission visits Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: U.N. human rights mission visits Afghanistan.

text.p: The United Nations special rapporteur on human rights for Afghanistan said on Thursday he was in the country to assess the situation, particularly the plight of women under the Taleban administration.
"I am here to assess the situation on the ground," said Special Rapporteur Professor Paik Choong-Hyun told Reuters.
Paik expressed concern about the long-term effects of the fundamentalist Islamic Taleban's policies towards women.
There has been frequent international criticism of the human rights record of the Taleban, particularly over women.
In the 75 per cent of Afghanistan they control, they have banned women from the workplace and closed girls' schools.
"The future of Afghanistan depends on the children of today. The quality of their mother's education will affect the quality of the children in the future," Paik said.
Paik, who arrived in Kabul earlier this week and will leave on January 14, is due to file a report at the end of the month.
A statement released last year by the United Nations special rapporteur on violence against women criticised the Taleban.

"The special rapporteur ... expresses her concern that the following human rights of Afghan women are threatened: the right to liberty and security of persons; the right to equal status and to be free from all forms of discrimination; the right to equal access to education, and the right to work," said the statement from Special Rapporteur Radhika Coomaraswamy.

The U.N. high commissioner for human rights, Jose Ayala- Lasso, sent a message to the leader of the Taleban in October saying their denial of women's access to education and work was against international conventions signed by Afghanistan.

"The international community is deeply concerned about the respect by the Taleban movement of all the commitments entered into by Afghanistan regarding the protection of all human rights, particularly those guaranteeing the basic rights of women including the girl child," Ayala-Lasso's statement said.
Afghanistan is a signatory to a number of legally binding international human rights instruments including the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.

The Taleban have defended their position, saying they are implementing Islamic law in the country. They have said they are not against women working or girls going to school, but that the conditions are not yet right.
"In principle, we are not against women's education or women working, but they do not have the right to work outside the home as long as sound opportunities are not provided.
"That requires security and the setting up of partitioned offices and transport systems for women," said Mullah Enayatullah Baligh of the Taleban's department for promoting good and suppressing vice.
Women are allowed to work in the medical field, but only under severe restrictions.
